paras: The Fulton church shooting was the killing of Nina (or Mina) Emmerson, a Black woman, by her husband, Jackson Emmerson, during a service at the Pilgrims' Rest Church in Fulton, Missouri, on the night of October 22, 1888. Emmerson was jailed amid reported "strong threats of lynching him," but no attack on the jail was reported, and early in November he broke out of the Fulton jail with another prisoner held for murder. A brief wire dispatch carried the shooting to papers across the country, and at least one headlined it as a case for lynching.

According to a Fulton dispatch printed in the Mexico Weekly Ledger, the shooting took place about 8 o'clock, while the choir of the Pilgrim's Rest (colored) Church was singing the opening hymn. Emmerson drew a revolver and fired at his wife without effect, and a second shot entered the back of her head and came out over her eye, killing her. The Ledger added that he "then fired two more shots into her body" before leaving the church, and a later Fulton report said he had shot her four times. The congregation stampeded, and the preacher jumped out of a second-story window. Emmerson afterward gave himself up to the authorities; the cause of the shooting was not known, and an inquest was under way the next day.

The wire dispatch said only that Emmerson was in jail and that "there are strong threats of lynching him," without saying who made them. The Ledger's version placed the talk among Fulton's Black residents: "The colored people are greatly excited, and talk of lynching is heard among them." No report of a crowd at the jail or of an attempt to seize him appears in the coverage.

A Fulton dispatch of November 8, printed in the Butler Weekly Times, reported that three prisoners had broken jail on Tuesday night between 8 and 11 o'clock. One of them, Wm. Reeves, returned the next morning to be locked up, leaving Robert J. Clanton, indicted for the murder of three men, and "Jack Emerson" at large. The county court offered a $200 reward for the capture and conviction of the two and described Emerson as 23 years old, "quite black," slender, stammering, and missing part of a finger on his right hand. Weekly news digests listed the escape of three murderers, Robert Clanton, T. T. Whitington and Jackson Emerson, from the Fulton jail on the 7th. No report of his recapture, of the inquest's finding, or of a trial was found.

The story moved as a special to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch from Fulton, which the Memphis Appeal credited in its version of October 24. The same text, usually headed "Killed His Wife in Church," ran that day in the New York Sun, the Indianapolis Journal and the Camden Evening Telegram, and in garbled form in the Silver State of Unionville, Nevada. Most versions called it a "sensational wife murder" and closed with "The parties were colored," while the Sun and the Camden paper identified Emmerson as "colored" in the first line instead. The Omaha Daily Bee printed it on October 25, and the Bismarck Weekly Tribune ran it on October 26 under the headline "Ripe for Judge Lynch."

The fuller Fulton account, which called Emmerson "the fiend," appeared in the Mexico Weekly Ledger and, as "Bloody Scene in a Church," in the Idaho News of November 3. In Olympia, the Washington Standard quoted the item in a November 9 editorial on church disorders and concluded that "it will soon be necessary to go to church armed." No paper reported the threats as more than talk, and none followed the case beyond the jail escape.

Reports differ on several details, beginning with the date: the Indianapolis Journal dated its dispatch October 22 and placed the shooting "last night," while the Sun, the Mexico Ledger and the later Fulton report point to Monday night, October 22. The wife's name appears as "Nina" in the wire and as "Mina" in the Ledger and the Washington Standard. The Fulton report dated the escape Tuesday night and counted two men still at large, whereas the digests gave the 7th and named three escaped murderers.

reader.title: Fulton church shooting
bases: A Black man jailed for killing his wife in church was the object of reported 'strong threats of lynching' (A1, A2, A12), but no mob action followed; the episode is a threatened lynching attached to an individual homicide.

No one was killed by a group: Nina Emmerson was shot by her husband alone (A1, A12), and the only collective action reported is talk or threats of lynching him, after which he escaped jail (A12, A18).

The shooting and the lynching threats are reported both in the Post-Dispatch wire (A1, A4) and in a separate, fuller Fulton dispatch (A12), and a later Fulton report confirms the killing and his escape (A18).
